body_markdown:
It's that time of year. Budgets are due, renewal notices are stacking up, and someone in a meeting just said, "Let's just roll it over to next year." Auto-renewing a vendor contract is easy, but it's also how mediocre partners quietly become permanent fixtures at your properties. Before you sign on for another year, give every partner a proper report card. Your residents, your on-site teams, and your budget will thank you.


Here's how to grade fairly, quickly, and with data instead of gut feelings.


##


**Why a Report Card, and Why Now?**


The end of the year is your leverage window. Contracts are open, budgets are taking shape, and your vendors want to keep your business. That makes it the perfect moment for a structured review, one that turns vague frustrations like "they're kind of slow" into specifics you can act on, like "they missed 4 of 12 scheduled turns in Q3."


But a report card isn't only about catching problems. It's also how you protect your stronger partners. Those who showed up all year deserve real recognition, and maybe a bigger slice of next year's work.


##


**The Six Subjects Every Vendor Should Be Graded On**


1.


**Reliability:** Did they show up when they said they would? For staffing partners, look at fill rates and time to fill. For service vendors, look at on-time completion. Reliability is the subject that matters most, because everything else depends on it.


2.


**Quality of work:** Were make-readies done right the first time? Did temporary leasing agents actually convert tours? Count callbacks, redo requests, and resident complaints tied to the vendor.


3.


**Responsiveness:** When something went sideways on a Friday afternoon, how fast did they answer? Track response times on urgent requests, not just routine ones. Anyone can be responsive when nothing is on fire.


4.


**Compliance and safety:** Are insurance certificates current? Have background checks been completed? Were safety incidents reported and resolved? This subject is pass or fail. A vendor who fails here doesn't get extra credit anywhere else.


5.


**Cost and value:** Compare invoices against the contract. Look for surprise fees, scope creep, and billing errors. Then ask the bigger question: did the price match the results?


6.


**Partnership:** This is the extra-credit column. Did they bring ideas, flag problems early, and understand your properties? Great partners know your portfolio almost as well as you do.


##


**Build a Simple Grading Scale**


**Grade**


**What it means**


**Renewal action**


A


Consistently exceeds expectations


Renew, and consider expanding scope


B


Meets expectations with minor gaps


Renew with clear goals for next year


C


Inconsistent or needs frequent follow-up


Renew short-term with a performance plan, or rebid


D


Regularly misses expectations


Rebid or replace


F


Failed compliance or safety


Replace


You can also weight the subjects to match your priorities. A maintenance staffing partner might weight reliability and quality more heavily, while a landscaping vendor might lean on quality and cost.


##


**Get Input From the People on the Ground**


Your on-site managers, maintenance supervisors, and leasing teams work with these vendors every day. Send a short survey with the six subjects and a 1 to 5 rating for each, as well as one open question: "What's one thing this vendor should do differently next year?"


Pair that feedback with hard numbers, including work order data, invoices, fill reports, and resident reviews. When the stories and the stats agree, you've got a clear grade. When they don't, it's time to dig a little deeper.


##


**Hold the Parent-Teacher Conference**


Share the report card with each vendor before the renewal window (even the A students). Walk through the grades, the evidence, and your expectations for the year ahead.


The best partners will welcome it, come back with a plan, and maybe even better terms. The ones who get defensive? That's a grade in itself.


You should also put agreed-upon goals into the new contract. Specific, measurable targets (like a fill rate or response time) give both sides something real to aim for and make next year's report card even easier to complete.


##


**Don’t Forget Your Staffing Partner**


Staffing often gets graded on one thing: price per hour. But the right staffing partner affects nearly every other grade on your list. A great temporary maintenance tech means faster turns


**,** and a sharp leasing professional means more signed leases, while a no-show means a scramble.


When you review your staffing partner, ask:


-


How quickly do they fill urgent and seasonal requests?


-


Do their associates arrive trained for property management work, from software to resident service?


-


Do they understand your local market and your properties?


-


Are they proactive about planning for peak leasing season and turn volume?

[BG Staffing](https://propmgtdiv.bgsf.com/) , property management is all we do. That focus shows up in the grades that matter: people who know the work, show up ready, and fit your teams from day one.


##


Make the Grade, Then Make the Call


A year-end report card takes a few hours of focused work. But skipping it can lock you into a whole year with the wrong partner, along with the missed turns, slow responses, and surprise invoices that come with it. So grade honestly, share the results openly, and renew with intention. Every contract you sign should reflect what you learned this year, not what you agreed to last year.


At the end of the day, your properties run on the people behind them. Residents notice when a unit is ready on time, when a maintenance request gets handled fast, and when the leasing office feels fully staffed. Make sure every partner on your roster earns their spot.
